cards.title: Treat conversion rate as the primary growth lever when ad costs rise
cards.summary: Doubling conversion rate beats doubling traffic because CRO lifts ROI on every future dollar of ad spend and compounds.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to allocate budget and effort between paid traffic acquisition and landing page/checkout conversion work for your store.
steps: Recognize that ad platforms run on auctions: competitors bid for the same eyeballs, so CPMs and CPCs tend to rise over time. The source cites year-over-year increases of roughly 61% on Meta, 185% on TikTok, and 75% on Google CPMs (14% on search CPCs) as an example of that trend, not a forecast.

Think of two ways to double revenue: double traffic, or double conversion rate. The source argues conversion is superior because a higher-converting page multiplies the return on all traffic you send later, and the gain persists after the campaign ends.

Before buying more traffic, audit whether the page is fundamentally optimized: does the above-the-fold section state who you are, what you sell and the customer's benefit in under 5 seconds? Fix structural gaps first, then scale spend.
Also model the downstream effect: a conversion-efficiency gain expands your LTV to CAC ratio, which in the source's framing lets you outbid competitors in ads and reinvest in the business.
Keep spend scaling gated on measured conversion performance rather than launching more campaigns into an unoptimized page.
caveats: The specific platform cost increases are the source's illustrative figures and change over time; verify current data.
A conversion lift only compounds if the traffic quality and offer stay comparable; it is not a substitute for product-market fit.

cards.title: Run one split test per week and let wins compound
cards.summary: Testing one element per week forces focus and produces a compounding record of what your audience responds to.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable landing page or PDP testing cadence for your store instead of ad-hoc redesigns.
steps: Hold a weekly marketing meeting and commit to a single split test per week, as the source does. One test forces you to pick the hypothesis most likely to move results rather than spreading effort across many ideas.

Log every test's result, win or lose, in a shared document with the hypothesis, the variant, and the measured outcome. The source treats this dataset as the real asset, because winning insights transfer to ads, positioning, and product decisions.

When a test wins, immediately design the next test to double down on that same winning idea before moving to an unrelated element. The source describes an ecommerce client where moving price lower on the product page and adding trust elements above it produced a 32% conversion gain, and adding more trust elements above the price produced a cumulative 88% gain.
Over a year (52 tests) and multiple years, the compounding record makes each subsequent hypothesis better informed, so conversion improves as a process, not by luck.
Inspect the current testing tool's setup each time, since interfaces and statistical reporting change.
caveats: One test per week assumes enough traffic for statistical significance; the source notes a business with tens of thousands of visitors per month can sustain it, and that under about 1,000 visitors per week you likely cannot.
Sequential wins from doubling down on one theme are source-reported case results, not guaranteed outcomes.

cards.title: Use an A/B calculator to set test duration on low-traffic stores
cards.summary: Low-traffic stores should calculate required sample size before testing, or make sequential changes measured with session recordings instead.
cards.use_when: Planning how many tests your store can realistically run per month given its traffic and current conversion rate.
steps: Enter your current traffic level and baseline conversion rate into an online A/B testing calculator before launching a test. The calculator returns how long the test must run and how many tests are realistically possible at your volume.
If you have fewer than roughly 1,000 visitors per week, the source says you realistically cannot run one statistically valid A/B test per week. Do not call a result a win on a sample that small.

For low-traffic stores in the range of about 10,000 to 20,000 visitors per month, the source's agency instead reviews objective behavioral data (the source mentions Microsoft Clarity session recordings and heatmaps) and makes changes based on observed friction, then measures what happens over time.

With this sequential approach, accept that you cannot attribute the change to a single element the way a 50/50 split would. Treat it as directional evidence and keep the change only if the metric holds after a full business cycle.
Re-run the calculator whenever traffic or conversion baseline shifts materially, since the required sample size changes.
caveats: Statistical significance thresholds and calculator interfaces vary by tool; verify the current tool's assumptions.
Sequential before/after changes are confounded by seasonality, promotions and traffic mix; the source explicitly frames them as an alternative to, not equivalent of, a true split test.

cards.title: Test the above-the-fold section first — it is the highest-leverage area
cards.summary: The top of the page is the only section 100% of visitors see and roughly 60% never scroll past it, so headline and hero image tests generate the largest gains.
cards.use_when: Choosing which page element to test next on a landing page, PDP, or homepage when you can only run one experiment.
steps: Treat the above-the-fold area (headline and the image below it) as the default testing target, especially in early optimization stages. The source advises spending the vast majority of early effort there.

Test the headline first, then the hero image underneath it. The source's agency says nearly all of the biggest conversion jumps come from these two elements, with headline tests producing lifts in the 60–80% range and above-the-fold tests reported as high as 130% across both B2B and ecommerce clients.

Justify prioritization with two facts the source cites: 100% of visitors see the above-the-fold area, and statistically about 60% never scroll past it, so changes below the fold are only ever seen by a minority.
Keep one change per test so you can attribute the lift to the headline or the image rather than a combined redesign.
Once the above-the-fold is strong, move budget and test slots to lower sections such as trust elements or product-detail modules.
caveats: The 60% no-scroll figure and the percentage lifts are source-reported approximations and case examples, not universal benchmarks.
Some product categories need scroll depth for considered purchases; test whether adding above-the-fold information changes scroll behavior.

cards.title: Write headlines that pass the 5-second who/what/benefit test
cards.summary: A headline must state who you are, what you do, and what's in it for the customer in under 5 seconds, with the benefit being the most important part.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the main headline and subheadline on a store homepage, landing page, or product page.
steps: Ask whether the headline clearly answers three questions: who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me. The third is the most important and the one most pages omit.
State the core benefit in concrete terms: does the offer save time, save money, reduce risk, or increase status? Make that legible within 5 seconds of landing.

Only after the benefit is nailed down, run variant tests on the headline itself, testing different phrasings of the value proposition or different framings of the end benefit. The source reports 60–80% conversion gains from headline tests alone.
Use the headline as the first place the Value Equation's dream outcome appears, and reinforce it in the body copy directly underneath.
Check that the subheadline and hero image do not contradict the headline's promise, since the three are seen together in the same 5-second window.
caveats: The 5-second rule and lift percentages come from the source's agency experience; treat as heuristic guides rather than measured thresholds.
Different awareness levels of traffic may need differently specific headlines; run variants rather than assuming one formulation.

cards.title: Use the 'so that' chain to find the deepest customer benefit
cards.summary: Repeatedly asking 'so that…' drills past the functional feature to the end outcome the customer actually wants.
cards.use_when: Developing headline, hero, or ad copy for your store when the first benefit you write sounds generic or feature-based.
steps: Start with what your product functionally does, then ask 'so that…' and answer it.

Continue the chain until the answer reaches an outcome the customer would recognize as valuable in their own life. The source's worked example: 'Warm up your emails so that you land in the inbox so that you close more deals so that you generate more revenue.'
Put the deepest outcome in the above-the-fold headline, and keep the intermediate steps in the supporting body copy to make the logic credible.

Apply the same chain to physical goods: for a table, the functional answer is 'something to put things on,' but the deeper outcome is 'when guests walk into my home they feel immediately impressed,' which reframes the purchase around status.

For consumer products, spend more time translating what the status or lifestyle outcome means to the buyer and how painful the lack of it has been; the source notes B2B buyers are easier to reach because the outcome is usually money and time.
caveats: Pushing too far up the chain can produce abstract claims that lose specificity and credibility; balance the deepest benefit with a concrete product fact.
The status-based framing is the source's example, not a universal rule for every category.

cards.title: Map the Value Equation to specific page elements
cards.summary: Hormozi's four-part value framework becomes page components: dream outcome in the headline, perceived likelihood under the CTA, time delay in copy and shipping, effort in 'done-for-you' wording.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing product page or landing page to find which value component is missing or weak.
steps: Dream Outcome: state the end goal explicitly in the main headline and subheadline above the fold. If the buyer wants to save time, make money, or lose weight, that outcome should be visible immediately.

Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (risk): place trust badges, guarantees, testimonials, case studies, free trials, no-credit-card terms or return policies directly below or around the CTA button. The source's example places free trial, fast setup, easy cancellation and API integrations under a SaaS CTA, and free 30-day returns, money-back guarantee, one-year warranty and free US shipping under an ecommerce add-to-cart button.

Time Delay: quantify how fast the buyer gets results or receives the product. Examples: a 'ships in 24 hours' line under the add-to-cart button, or 'get funded fast' on a mortgage CTA. The longer the perceived delay, the less valuable the offer reads.
Effort and Sacrifice: write copy that states what the customer will not have to do, such as 'we reach out to thousands of influencers so that you don't have to.'
Score your page against all four components and fix the weakest one first rather than rewriting everything at once.
caveats: The source's example lifts (e.g. a 30% conversion gain from adding guarantee badges, from A/B testing) are case-study results, not expected averages.
B2B pages often need less status framing because money and time outcomes are obvious; consumer pages may need more.

cards.title: De-risk the purchase with guarantees directly under the CTA
cards.summary: Placing trust badges, guarantees and return terms next to the buy button removes purchase uncertainty and, in the source's test, lifted conversion 30%.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a PDP or landing page where visitors hesitate or abandon near the add-to-cart or signup button.
steps: List the main uncertainties a buyer has at the moment of clicking buy: will it arrive, can I return it, is it guaranteed, does it work with my setup.

Place explicit assurances directly under or beside the CTA button rather than in a distant footer. Typical ecommerce set: free 30-day return, 100% money-back guarantee, one-year warranty, free shipping. Typical software set: free trial, fast setup, easy cancellation, integration logos.

If price is the objection, restructure the page so trust-building elements appear above the price, not after it. The source's ecommerce client saw a 32% conversion gain from lowering price position and adding trust above it, then a cumulative 88% gain after adding more trust elements above the price.
Run the badge set as a single A/B test against the page without badges; the source reports a 30% lift from adding guarantee badges under the add-to-cart button.
After a win, extend the same trust messaging into ad creative and email to keep the promise consistent across touchpoints.
caveats: Badges must reflect real policy; citing guarantees you don't honor creates refund and dispute problems.
Badge sets that work for physical goods may need different specifics for services or subscriptions; test your own set.

cards.title: Quantify delivery and result timelines in copy and button labels
cards.summary: Reducing perceived time-to-result increases value; state shipping speed or result timelines in the copy and CTA, not just in policy pages.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, shipping messaging, or CTA labels for a store where fulfillment speed or time-to-outcome is a purchase driver.
steps: Find the time-related anxiety in your category — when will it arrive, how long until I see results — and answer it at the point of decision.
On ecommerce pages, place shipping speed under the add-to-cart button, e.g. 'ships in 24 hours', alongside secure-checkout reassurance.

On outcome-based products, quantify both amount and duration in the headline, as in the source's weight-loss example, 'lose 30 lbs in 90 days' — this states the dream outcome and the time delay together.
Use design as well as copy: a CTA button reading 'get funded fast' carries the time message without extra paragraph text, per the source's mortgage-lending example.
Test timeline messaging as its own variable, separate from price or image, so you can see how much of the lift comes from speed perception.
caveats: Do not promise timelines your logistics cannot meet; unmet speed claims drive returns and complaints.
The source notes that few companies quantify timelines properly, so this is often an untested gap rather than a proven winner for your store.

cards.title: Write 'done-for-you' copy to reduce perceived effort and sacrifice
cards.summary: Stating explicitly what the customer will not have to do lowers the effort component of value, especially for services and complex products.
cards.use_when: Writing hero or feature copy for a managed service, subscription, or product that replaces manual work your customer dislikes.
steps: Run customer interviews to find the manual, repetitive or unpleasant tasks your customer associates with getting the outcome. The source's influencer-agency research found users frustrated by manually contacting large numbers of influencers.
Turn that finding into a headline that names the eliminated work: 'we reach out to thousands of influencers so that you don't have to.'
Extend the same logic to service elements: white-glove delivery, assembly, setup, onboarding, or migration performed for the buyer rather than by them.
Place the effort-reduction message high on the page, since it functions as part of the value proposition rather than a feature detail.
Pair the promise with evidence, such as volume numbers or process descriptions, so the claim reads as credible rather than dismissive.
caveats: The source's examples are its own clients; the conversion impact of effort-reduction copy varies by category.
Overpromising 'we do everything' can create operational and expectation problems; keep the claim within what you deliver.

cards.title: Choose hero images that reinforce the value proposition
cards.summary: The hero image should visually demonstrate who you are and what you deliver; a weak or generic image is a common source of lost conversions.
cards.use_when: Selecting or testing the main image under the headline on a landing page, PDP, or homepage.
steps: Check whether the current hero image communicates the core value proposition on its own. The source's 'before' example was described as a boring image conveying nothing about the offer.
Identify what visual proof your product can show: outputs, customer usage, social proof at scale, or the end state the buyer wants.

Build the replacement image around that proof. For the influencer agency example, the agency assembled the client work produced with influencers into a collage or carousel to demonstrate social proof at scale, producing a reported 78% conversion gain from that image test alone.
Test the image as its own variable, separate from the headline, so you can attribute the result.
Once an image concept wins on the page, reuse the same concept in ad creative; the source reports a large click-through-rate increase after applying the carousel concept to ads.
caveats: Image tests can shift perceived audience or brand tone, so watch impact on lead quality, not just conversion count.
The 78% figure is one client case and depends on the original image being poor.

cards.title: Treat CRO results as transferable customer research, not just a page metric
cards.summary: Every winning or losing test reveals what resonates with your audience and can be redeployed across ads, positioning, and product decisions.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to do with test results beyond keeping or reverting the variant on your store's pages.
steps: Log each test as a hypothesis about the customer, not just an element change: record what you believed would resonate and whether it did.

For winning tests, extract the underlying insight and inject it into other channels: ad creative angles, value proposition framing, product naming, UX changes, and feature ideas. The source's example carried the winning carousel image concept from the landing page into ads and saw a large click-through-rate increase.
For losing tests, treat the result as evidence to avoid that message in marketing rather than discarding the test.
Feed the insight back into the next landing page test so each weekly experiment builds on audience knowledge rather than starting fresh.
Use the accumulated record to make positioning decisions that span page, ads, and product messaging.
caveats: Transferring a landing-page insight to ads or product assumes similar audience and context; validate in the new channel rather than assuming the same lift.
Insights decay as audience and competitive context change; revisit them periodically.

cards.title: Frame premium physical goods around status, not features
cards.summary: The dream outcome for a consumer product can be a felt status shift, which justifies a price far above the functional value of the materials.
cards.use_when: Positioning and pricing a premium or discretionary physical product in your store where competing on materials alone drives price comparisons.
steps: Identify the functional description of your product and then name the deeper outcome the buyer wants. For a table, the functional answer is 'a surface to put things on'; the status outcome is 'guests feel immediately impressed when they walk in.'

Translate the status outcome into risks and objections: if status is the goal, the risk is that the product fails to signal it, so show evidence that the style or trend is understood and valued (for example, demonstrating that the look is a recognized trend).

Reduce the friction around delivery and setup for heavy or complex goods: offer white-glove delivery, doorway fitting, on-site assembly, and near-immediate arrival so the buyer can use it for a specific occasion.
Tie all four value components to the status framing so the buyer is willing to pay for how much the status is worth to them, rather than for the wood or materials.
Because the source notes consumer buyers need more translation than B2B buyers, spend additional copy explaining the meaning of the status shift and the pain of lacking it.
caveats: The table example is the source's hypothetical illustration, not a tested campaign result.
Status framing can alienate buyers seeking value or durability; test against a functional framing for your audience.

cards.title: Always test the headline before any other page element
cards.summary: Headline tests produce the largest and most reliable gains, so make the headline the first and most frequent test on every page.
cards.use_when: Deciding the first experiment to run on a new or underperforming store page.
steps: Start every optimization sequence with the headline, since it is seen by 100% of visitors and sits in the above-the-fold area the source treats as highest leverage.
Generate variants that express different value propositions or different phrasings of the same end benefit, rather than cosmetic edits like word order.
Verify each variant still answers who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me within 5 seconds before spending test budget on it.
Keep a running list of winning headline framings, because they transfer to ad copy, email subject lines and product descriptions.
Only after the headline has been optimized, move test slots to the hero image and then to lower-page elements.
caveats: The 60–80% lift figures come from the source's agency experience and vary with the original headline's weakness.
Low-traffic stores may need to run headline changes sequentially with over-time measurement rather than true split tests.

The source's 'before' example was described as a boring image conveying nothing about the offer.", "Identify what visual proof your product can show: outputs, customer usage, social proof at scale, or the end state the buyer wants.", "Build the replacement image around that proof. For the influencer agency example, the agency assembled the client work produced with influencers into a collage or carousel to demonstrate social proof at scale, producing a reported 78% conversion gain from that image test alone.", "Test the image as its own variable, separate from the headline, so you can attribute the result.", "Once an image concept wins on the page, reuse the same concept in ad creative; the source reports a large click-through-rate increase after applying the carousel concept to ads."], "caveats": ["Image tests can shift perceived audience or brand tone, so watch impact on lead quality, not just conversion count.", "The 78% figure is one client case and depends on the original image being poor."], "tags": ["landing-pages", "creative-strategy", "conversion-optimization", "product-page", "acquisition", "experiment-design"]}, {"title": "Treat CRO results as transferable customer research, not just a page metric", "summary": "Every winning or losing test reveals what resonates with your audience and can be redeployed across ads, positioning, and product decisions.", "use_when": "Deciding what to do with test results beyond keeping or reverting the variant on your store's pages.", "steps": ["Log each test as a hypothesis about the customer, not just an element change: record what you believed would resonate and whether it did.", "For winning tests, extract the underlying insight and inject it into other channels: ad creative angles, value proposition framing, product naming, UX changes, and feature ideas. The source's example carried the winning carousel image concept from the landing page into ads and saw a large click-through-rate increase.", "For losing tests, treat the result as evidence to avoid that message in marketing rather than discarding the test.", "Feed the insight back into the next landing page test so each weekly experiment builds on audience knowledge rather than starting fresh.", "Use the accumulated record to make positioning decisions that span page, ads, and product messaging."], "caveats": ["Transferring a landing-page insight to ads or product assumes similar audience and context; validate in the new channel rather than assuming the same lift.", "Insights decay as audience and competitive context change; revisit them periodically."], "tags": ["landing-pages", "customer-research", "conversion-optimization", "creative-strategy", "positioning", "measurement"]}, {"title": "Frame premium physical goods around status, not features", "summary": "The dream outcome for a consumer product can be a felt status shift, which justifies a price far above the functional value of the materials.", "use_when": "Positioning and pricing a premium or discretionary physical product in your store where competing on materials alone drives price comparisons.", "steps": ["Identify the functional description of your product and then name the deeper outcome the buyer wants. 07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of Alex Hormozi's approach to Conversion Rate Optimization (CRO) and landing page design. Covers the financial impact of CRO, systematic A/B testing (specifically "above the fold"), and applying the "Value Equation" (Dream Outcome, Perceived Likelihood of Achievement, Time Delay, and Effort/Sacrifice) to landing page copy and layout. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or ad account scaling -> 06-MEA • Brand strategy, logo design, or foundational positioning -> 04-BRD

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details how to directly apply a well-known behavioral framework (The Value Equation) to specific landing page elements, demonstrating how to systematically test and optimize the "above the fold" section to maximize ROI on ad spend. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, landing pages, Alex Hormozi, Value Equation, A/B testing, above the fold, copywriting, B2B landing pages, e-commerce landing pages] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the ROI of CRO / explaining that as ad costs (CPMs and CPCs) rise across Meta, TikTok, and Google, doubling the conversion rate is mathematically superior and more cost-effective than attempting to double traffic; systematic A/B testing / the importance of testing only one element per week to compound wins over time, using an AB testing calculator to ensure statistical significance for low-traffic sites; optimizing the "above the fold" / why the topmost section of a landing page is the highest-leverage area to test (since 100% of visitors see it and 60% never scroll past it), focusing primarily on testing the headline and the hero image; headline copywriting / ensuring the headline answers "who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me" in under 5 seconds, using the "so that" principle to arrive at the deepest customer benefit; the Value Equation on landing pages / translating Hormozi's four-part framework into page elements: (1) Dream Outcome: explicitly stating the end goal in the main headline; (2) Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (Risk): using trust badges, guarantees, and testimonials below the CTA to de-risk the purchase; (3) Time Delay: quantifying how fast the user will get results or receive the product (e.g., "Get funded fast" or "Ships in 24 hours"); (4) Effort and Sacrifice: writing copy that highlights "done-for-you" aspects or emphasizes how the product eliminates manual labor (e.g., "We reach out to thousands of influencers so you don't have to").

Look for.

The "Above the Fold" Rule: The statistical reality that 100% of visitors see the top of a page, but 60% never scroll down, making the main headline and hero image the most profitable elements to split-test.

The "So That" Principle: A copywriting technique to find the true Dream Outcome by asking "so that..." multiple times (e.g., "Warm up your emails so that you land in the inbox so that you close more deals").

The Value Equation Mapping: How to map Hormozi's framework directly to page elements: Dream Outcome (Headline), Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (Trust badges/guarantees under the CTA button), Time Delay (Shipping or result timelines), and Effort/Sacrifice (Copy explicitly stating what the user won't have to do).

Skip. Mentions of Microsoft Clarity, general complaints about rising ad costs on Meta/TikTok, and the podcast host's promotional intro/outro to other videos.

Scope mix. 20% baseline (general CRO definitions), 80% growth (advanced landing page psychology, specific A/B testing methodologies, and applying the Value Equation to UX design). Volume. ~400 words.

Alex Hermoszi is one of the most successful businessmen of our time. And he's exited multiple businesses for over eight figures. And part of the reason he got there is because of his conversion rates on his landing pages and websites. As someone who's built over 400 landing pages in over 80 niches, I was naturally curious to see what he had to say when it comes to building landing pages. Throughout this video, we'll listen to what Alex has to say about building landing pages, and then we'll see how can we apply that knowledge in order to make ones that convert. What I want to give you today is one very, very simple hack that we've used to consistently improve our marketing. Neil Patel said in one of his keynote speeches that he believes that the future of marketing is going to exist in CRO, so conversion rate optimization. And he said that because, you know, the prices are going to only consistently go up. Most platforms are based on an auction, which means that it's just multiple businesses competing for the same eyeballs. And so the people who are better able to convert those eyeballs are going to be the ones who are going to be able to out compete and win. To help you really grasp the significance of what Alex is trying to say here, the cost of virtually every ad platform has skyrocketed over the last several years. And as Alex said, the cost just continues to increase yearover-year. Meta ad costs have increased 61% year-over-year. Tik Tok has increased by a whopping 185%. Google saw CPMs increase by 75% while search ad cost per clicks were up by 14%. So when Alex says that the future of marketing is conversion rate optimization, I couldn't agree more and I can't stress how important it is to understand this. Long gone are the days where you can just throw up a landing page on Meta or Google Ads and just expect it to generate you leads. This is literally what I encounter on a daily basis. I'll get companies come to us all the time complaining about low conversion rates on their website or landing pages. And when I go and take a look, I can immediately identify the reason why. And it's because their landing pages or websites are not fundamentally optimized for conversions in the first place. So, they're spending all this money and they're burning cash and sending money down the drain. Everyone loves to obsess over getting traffic, but never conversions. And as Alex mentioned, the companies that are able to out compete and win in the marketplace are the ones that are able to better convert the same traffic than their competitors. I always like to say to people, you have two different ways of doubling your revenue. The first way is you can double your traffic or the second way is you can double your conversion rate. And I will take doubling your conversion rate any day of the week because when you double your conversion rate and you drive more traffic to that same landing page, your revenue and ROI that you generate is also amplified. And I'm talking from experience when I say this. We've helped clients like this literally double their conversion rate just through conversion optimization alone. Every week what we do is we have our marketing meeting and we do one split test. Just one. And that's because everyone wants to test a 100 things. But what it does is it forces us to be very very focused on the one thing that we think is going to drive the highest result for us. This is the biggest thing that I feel holds a lot of brands back from doing more conversion optimization and it's that there's so many different things they want to test and they just don't know where to start. As Alex suggests, just make it simple. Just focus on a couple things at a time and just focus in getting in the habit of testing and becoming consistent in the first place. One thing to note that's not mentioned is the frequency of testing. Being able to do one split test a week will very much depend on your traffic levels. Presumably, someone like Alex is probably generating tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of visitors to his website and landing pages every single month. So, he actually has sufficient traffic levels to constitute one AB test per week. But if you have less than a,000 visitors a week, you realistically cannot do one test per week because you won't get statistically significant results. What we do at our agency is we use an AB testing calculator. There's a ton online. I'll put one in the description, but this will basically help you determine how long should you run your AB test and how many AB tests can you realistically run based on your traffic and conversion levels at the time. You also don't have to do testing via the form of an AB test. For our lower traffic clients, like let's say 10 to 20,000 visitors a month, what we'll often do is we'll make changes based on objective data that we collect in Microsoft Clarity and then measure what happens over time. But it's not in the traditional form of an AB test where we're splitting traffic 50/50. But the basic premise that Alex is saying of staying consistent with your testing is super important. Thing is is that when you do this every single week for 52 weeks in a row and you do that for 5 years, your process just gets better and better and better. those increases in conversion compound. What Alex is basically saying here is that as you start running AB test, you'll quickly start to pick up data on winning test and losing test. And the beautiful thing about this is that no matter what the result is, you can take those data points and those results and basically create a snowball effect where your results really start to compound over time. For example, for one of our e-commerce clients, they received a lot of objections around the price of their product. It wasn't necessarily that the product was expensive, but it was just expensive relative to other competitors in the market. What we ended up doing was we moved the price of the product down on the product page and we put a bunch of trust building elements above the price of the product. And so the first test that we ran netted a 32% increase in the conversion rate. Then we thought, how could we double down on this winning test? And so we added more trust building elements before the price. And that single hypothesis netted us a cumulative 88% increase in the conversion rate. So it's massive increases in conversions once you find one winning idea or one winning hypothesis. I'll give you the two biggest things that we look at. The first thing, this sounds obvious and simple, but people don't do it, is we simply split test the headlines on our landing pages. That's it. The next thing that we'll split test is going to be the image that is underneath of the headline. Because what we've seen from the vast majority of all of the tests that we've done is that almost all of the juice that's going to come, the biggest jumps in conversion rate happen above the fold. Testing the above the fold has historically gotten us the best ROI as well. And we've seen conversion increases by upwards of 130% by testing the above the fold. And we've seen this across both our B2B clients and our e-commerce clients as well. The above the fold is the topmost area of any page. It's the first thing that people will see. And there's two things that you need to understand when it comes to the above the fold. The first thing is that the above the fold is the only section on any page that you can guarantee with certainty that 100% of people will see. The second thing is that statistically 60% of people will never scroll past the above the fold section. That is why, as Alex suggests, the above the fold is the most critical area to test and it's where most people should be spending 99% of their efforts optimizing in the beginning stages. So, he mentions testing the headline, but you may be wondering what actually do I test. The first thing I would ask yourself is, does your headline clearly articulate who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me? And that last part is the most important. Does your headline clearly articulate what is that benefit and core differentiator of your product and service? How does your product or service actually benefit me in my day-to-day life? Does it save me time? Does it save me money? That needs to be clearly articulated in 5 seconds or less. Only when you nail that down, you can then focus on testing different headline variations which are going to basically be different variations of your value prop or different ways of saying the end benefit. We've seen conversion increases at our agency of upwards of 60 to 80% just by testing the headline on the above the fold section. The other thing he talks about is images. Your image should help to reinforce your core value prop and it should also subtly convey and articulate who you are and what you do. A great practical example of this is an AB test that we ran for influence hunter. They're an influencer marketing agency and they create a lot of UGC on behalf of their clients in partnering with influencers. before we ran an AB test, their before version just had a boring image. They didn't really convey anything about their value prop. But what we identified was that they had a lot of content that they produced for their clients in collaboration with influencers. So, we took all that content and we put it into this creative collage or carousel to reinforce their value prop of creating social proof at scale. Just from that image test alone, we saw a 78% increase in the conversion rate. Three, CRO improvements. And this was the largest company we have in the portfolio. So we got a plus 20% CRO test improvement which is a monster win. We got a 50% lift and then we got a 28% lift. So we had three mega wins. How valuable is that to the company? Tremendously valuable because things that are efficiency improvements typically are longasting. What's cool about that is that when you have an efficiency improvement, it means your LTV to CAC ratio expands which allows you to spend more money in advertising, more money in talent acquisition all the way around the business. It literally just makes the business stronger and is a competitive mode. I love this by Alex. A lot of people will look at CRO one-dimensionally and they'll just look at it from a short-term lens perspective that, oh, if I increase my conversion rate, I can then extract more value out of my marketing. That is literally just one out of the many benefits when it comes to testing on your landing page. As Alex mentioned, CRO is the one lever that can affect all aspects of your business. What you have to realize is that when you're doing CRO, you're actually collecting data on what tests win and what tests lose. And you're quite literally testing what is resonating with your audience and what isn't resonating. The biggest thing it helps with, which is often overlooked, is the data collection portion. When you do CRO and you see tests that win or lose, you're quite literally collecting data on what resonates with your audience and what doesn't. The beautiful thing about that is that that insight from your winning test is literally transferable to all other aspects of your business. You can start injecting that into your advertising material, your value proposition, the UX of your product, coming up with new features or ideas, it's transferable everywhere. And on the flip side, if you have data on test at lost, you can then stray away from using that in your marketing efforts. The best example I can give is influence hunter. We took that same concept of the carousel image and we actually applied it to their ads. And we saw a massive increase in the click-through rate of their ads. The value equation has four components, and I'm not going to go super deep on it, but I'll just walk you through it real quick. So, you've got the dream outcome, which is what's the big thing that people want. So, in this instance, it'd be they want to make more money in their gym. They might want to lose weight. They might want to have a fix their relationship. They might want to look cool in front of their friends. The next is the perceived likelihood of achievement or the equal opposite of that is risk. How likely is it that when I buy this thing, I get what I want? Which when he asked the question, well, how likely is it? This is what he's teasing out. Alex Heroszy's value equation is directly correlated with landing page optimization. When we look at the first two items here, the first thing is the dream outcome. What is that dream end state or dream goal that your target audience really wants to achieve? That dream outcome needs to be immediately articulated in your headline and your sub headline above the fold. Do they want to save time? Do they want to make more money? Do they want to close more deals? Whatever it is, it needs to be immediately articulated and we will go through some examples soon. The next part is reducing the perceived risk. Do you have case studies and testimonials to back up what you're saying? Do you have a free trial? Or maybe you have no credit card required if you're a B2B or SAS company. Or maybe you have a return policy if you're an e-commerce firm. Whatever it is, you need to reduce that perceived risk for your customers. The next question is time. How long is it going to take between when I start and when I get? And the longer that is, the less valuable the thing is. And then you have effort and sacrifice, which is how hard am I going to have to try? What am I going to have to start doing that I don't want to do or stop doing that I do want to do? In a hypothetical example, you'd want something that would be immediate, be no effort. It would be guaranteed, and it would be exactly what they want, the way they want it. People will read the copy on your landing page and be thinking, "How long will it take me to actually achieve that result?" You need to quantify the result as much as possible and really help articulate how long it's going to take somebody to achieve that result. The effort and sacrifice component is communicating through your copy and your design how much effort is it going to take somebody to achieve their dream outcome. We'll go through some actionable examples very shortly, so just keep watching. So, let's say I sell tables. How can we position our thing separately from other people? Now, if the dream outcome for that table is not, okay, I just need to have something that I could put stuff on top of. The dream outcome might be when people walk into my home, they feel immediately impressed. So, now we're actually relating this to status because B2B is actually pretty easy. It's just this is how much money it is. And then the rest of your time is trying to make it easier for them, less risky, and faster. business to consumer. Sometimes you need to spend a little bit more time on translating what this status increase might mean for them and how meaningful that is or the reverse how terrible and painful it's been to lack this status. Let's start with some examples of the dream outcome and what Alex is referring to as status which is effectively positioning your product or service as valuable. And so starting with B2B, we want to think about what is it that my target audience actually desires. So the first example here is Inboxy. This is a client that we worked with and they are basically an email deliverability and warm-up tool. On their landing page here, you can see they have email deliverability and warm-up tool that is explaining the who you are, what you do. The headline needs to clearly articulate the what is in it for me. The way that I like to think of it is using the so that principle. You're warming up your emails so that you can land more emails in the inbox so that you can close more deals, so that you can generate more revenue. Just using that so that principle basically helps you get to the deeper why and the deeper benefit. And that is what that end goal is ultimately for your target audience. In the body text here, it's helping to reinforce that core value prop. The only inbox warm-up solution that utilizes a private network of headless browsers. And this is the perceived likelihood of achieving that dream outcome. It says to truly guarantee you better deliverability. On the e-commerce side, this is an example here, AVI, which is a weight loss product. right at the very top of the site, lose 30 lbs in 90 days. They're highlighting both the time aspect in 90 days and they're quantifying it. Lose 30 lbs. That is that dream outcome I care about, which is losing weight. So, if we have this big expensive, nice table, then we say, okay, here's the status. Now, the risk of this not happening. This is where we might show trends of this being a hot thing that many people understand the value of. So, the risk of them not getting the status is lowered. This is an example of a landing page that we've done for a client scrubby. Right underneath that CTA button, we have free trial, fast setup, easy cancellation, and it integrates with all these APIs. So, we're completely de-risking the proposition of their software product. On the e-commerce side, we did this for our client, Parcel Safety, where we added in these badges underneath the add to cart button. So, we have free 30-day return, 100% money back guarantee, one-year warranty, and free US shipping. All of the uncertainty that I have around buying the product is addressed upfront. Again, it's derisking the whole proposition of buying this product in the first place. We actually ran this as an AB test. So, they didn't even have these badges to begin with. And we saw a 30% lift in conversions just from that AB test alone. The time is like, hey, I can have this at your house by the end of today. That would be something like, wow, this could happen right in time for this dinner party I have or my boss is coming to my house. So, now moving over to the time principle, we want to reduce the time from what we think something will take to get to that end result. So for inboxy, we're actually highlighting this in their copy. And I see very few companies actually do this properly, which is quantifying it and basically closing that gap and telling people how quickly can you expect to receive results. Another great way of doing this is that you don't only have to do this in the copy. You can actually do this when it comes to the design of the landing page as well. Ryden is a mortgage lending company that we worked with and on their landing page, look at the CTA button here, get funded fast because that is a big pain point of their target audience which is getting fast funding. So again, we're highlighting the time aspect here and we're saying get funded fast. Just subconsciously highlighting the time aspect and reducing the time gap between how long is it going to take for me to achieve my desired result or desired outcome. On the e-commerce side, it's pretty easy to do this. You just want to highlight the shipping policy over here. You can see underneath the add to card for prepared hero. They have guaranteed secure checkout and they also have ships in 24 hours. And then effort and sacrifices. Don't worry, we have a white glove service that will make sure that we can fit it into your doorways even though it's this massive thing and we will assemble it there for you. You just need to say yes right now and it will be there by the end of the night and you can have dinner on it when you have your guest tomorrow. Now, we've tied them buying to all of the value components to getting them to then be willing to spend $20,000 because it's not about the wood. It's not about the table. It's about how much status is worth to them within this context. So when you're thinking about reducing the effort and sacrifice, the best way to do this is through your copy on your landing page. We did this landing page for influence center and on their landing page we have over here we reach out to thousands of influencers so that you don't have to. That headline is super impactful as far as reducing the perceived effort and sacrifice that is required to basically work with influence hunter. There's this common pain point when we were interviewing users for influence hunters website and we were doing user research. People expressed a lot of frustration around having to manually reach out to tons of influencers to basically get their products in the hands of these influencers to then post. Hermosy's advice is definitely strong, but now that you have his advice in mind and you understand it on a theoretical level, you need to actually apply the information. And it's hard to do that without a step-by-step guide on setting up a landing page. Click here to go to the next video where I show you the four proven steps that I use to consistently build million-dollar landing pages over and over again so that you can take those and combine them from what Alex Hermoszy's advice on those are and make your own killer landing page that will make you millions. See you in the next one.
